The test image shows a wheat head (spike) with dark/blackened spikelets. The grains appear to be replaced by dark masses throughout the spike, with intact awns and rachis. This pattern strongly suggests a smut disease — either Loose Smut or Dwarf Bunt.

My top candidate is **Loose_Smut**, where grains are converted to dark powdery teliospore masses. Let me view one reference image to confirm.

The reference image files are not accessible on disk. I'll rely entirely on my visual analysis of the test image.

**Visual Analysis:**
- Wheat head (spike) clearly showing dark/blackened spikelets throughout
- Dark masses appear to have replaced the grain kernels
- Awns are still intact and spreading outward
- Rachis structure remains intact
- The darkening is distributed across essentially all spikelets in the head
- No pink/orange coloring (rules out Head Scab/Fusarium)
- No bleached/white spikelets (rules out Head Scab)

**Key Differentiation:**
- **Loose Smut**: Entire spike converted to dark powdery teliospore masses, grains completely replaced, rachis and awns remain
- **Dwarf Bunt**: Dark bunt balls replace grains but glumes remain more intact, plants often stunted
- **Head Scab**: Pink/bleached spikelets, not dark throughout

The pattern in the test image — with the entire head converted to dark masses while the awns and rachis structure remain — is most characteristic of **Loose Smut** (Ustilago tritici), where the fungus destroys and replaces grain tissue with dark teliospores.
